questions.question: What are argument matchers in Mockito and how do you use them?
questions.title: Mockito Argument Matchers | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Argument matchers** let you stub and verify with flexible patterns instead of exact values. `any()` matches any argument. `eq(value)` matches a specific value. `anyString()`, `anyInt()`, `any(ClassName.class)` match by type. Mix matchers and exact values: all args must be matchers if any is.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Mockito stubbing and verification with matchers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing matcher and exact value arguments: when(mock.method(any(), 'literal')) causes MissingMethodInvocationException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the 'all or none' rule: if any argument uses a matcher, all must use matchers (wrap literals with eq())

sections.title: Flexible Argument Matching
sections.content: `when(repo.findByName(anyString())).thenReturn(List.of(user))` — matches any string argument. `verify(emailService).send(eq("admin@example.com"), any(EmailRequest.class))` — first arg must be exactly this email, second can be any EmailRequest. **The rule**: if ANY argument uses a matcher, ALL arguments must use matchers — wrap literals with `eq()`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- any(): matches any object (including null in some versions)
- any(ClassName.class): type-safe match
- anyString(), anyInt(), anyLong(), anyBoolean(): type-specific
- eq(value): exact value match — use when mixing with other matchers
- ArgumentMatchers.isNull(), isNotNull()
- startsWith(), contains(), endsWith(): String matchers
- argThat(predicate): custom matching logic
- Rule: all or none — can't mix matchers with raw values

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Argument matchers let me stub and verify without specifying exact argument values. any() matches any argument, any(ClassName.class) is type-safe, and there are type-specific ones like anyString and anyLong. The critical rule is: if any argument uses a matcher, all arguments must use matchers. So if I have a two-argument method and want to match the first broadly but the second exactly, I wrap the exact value with eq() — which is itself a matcher. argThat lets me define custom predicate logic for complex matching. Forgetting this rule causes a MissingMethodInvocationException which can be confusing if you don't know why.

questions.question: How do you use argThat() for custom argument matching in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito argThat Custom Matcher | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`argThat(predicate)`** accepts any argument that satisfies the predicate. Use it when built-in matchers aren't expressive enough — for example, matching an Order only if its total exceeds 100 and status is PENDING.

interviewer_intent.testing: Advanced Mockito matching for domain-specific verification
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using eq() with complex objects that rely on equals() that hasn't been implemented
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Combine argThat with a named method reference or named predicate for readable test code

sections.title: Custom Predicate Matching
sections.content: `verify(repository).save(argThat(order -> order.getTotal().compareTo(new BigDecimal("100")) > 0 && order.getStatus() == OrderStatus.PENDING))`. The lambda receives the argument and returns true if it matches. If false, the verification fails. For complex predicates: extract to a named method `verify(repo).save(argThat(this::isValidNewOrder))` for readability.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- argThat(Predicate): lambda or method reference
- Returns true: argument matches, test passes
- Returns false: argument doesn't match, test fails
- Use when: eq() requires equals(), which may not be implemented
- Use when: partial field matching without full equals
- Named predicate: improves readability of verify calls
- Also works with when() stubbing
- Type-specific: intThat(), longThat(), doubleThat()

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: argThat takes a predicate — a lambda or method reference that returns true if the argument matches. I use it when the built-in matchers aren't expressive enough — for example, when I want to verify that a repository.save was called with an Order object that has a specific status and a total above a threshold. I write the condition as a lambda that accesses the object's fields. For readability I'll often extract the predicate into a named method. It's also useful when the object doesn't have a meaningful equals implementation — eq() relies on equals() which might not be implemented for domain objects.

questions.question: How do Mockito argument matchers work with the verify() method?
questions.title: Mockito Argument Matchers with verify | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use argument matchers in `verify()` to assert that a method was called with arguments matching a pattern.** This is more flexible than requiring exact values — especially when the argument is a complex object where you only care about specific properties.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Verifying with any() when you should assert the specific value — hides bugs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the balance: use specific matchers when the argument matters for correctness, use any() when it truly doesn't matter

sections.title: Flexible Verification Assertions
sections.content: `verify(emailService).sendWelcomeEmail(eq("john@example.com"), any(String.class))` — first arg must be this exact email, second arg can be any string. `verify(repo, times(2)).findByCategory(any(Category.class))` — called twice with any Category. Use specific values when they matter for correctness; use any() when the exact value is irrelevant to the behavior being tested.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Matchers in verify(): same rules as in when() — all or none
- Use eq() for values that matter for correctness
- Use any() for args where the exact value doesn't matter
- Use argThat() for complex conditions
- Overly permissive (all any()): hides bugs
- Overly strict (all eq() on complex objects): brittle
- Balance: specific on meaningful args, any() on incidental args
- Combine with times(), never(), atLeastOnce()

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use argument matchers in verify when I want to assert on specific aspects of the call without over-specifying. For example, when verifying an email was sent I'll use eq on the recipient address — that's what matters — and any on the email body if the exact content is tested elsewhere. I avoid using any on everything in verify because that becomes a meaningless assertion — I'm just checking that some method was called, not that it was called correctly. The balance is: be specific on the arguments that define correctness, and use any or argThat for complex objects where I'm only testing specific fields through ArgumentCaptor.

questions.question: What is the difference between any() and any(ClassName.class) in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito any() vs any(Class) | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`any()` matches any argument including null. `any(ClassName.class)` matches any non-null argument of that type.** In Mockito 2+, `any()` does not match null — use `isNull()` or `nullable(ClassName.class)` explicitly for null matching.

interviewer_intent.testing: Null handling subtleties in Mockito matchers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using any() expecting it to match null — in Mockito 2+ it doesn't by default
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Mockito 1 vs Mockito 2 behavior change for null handling

sections.title: Type Safety and Null Handling
sections.content: In **Mockito 1**: `any()` matched anything including null. In **Mockito 2+**: `any()` matches any object but NOT null (strictly non-null). `any(OrderClass.class)` is type-safe — matches non-null OrderClass instances. For null: use `isNull()`. For nullable (null or type): use `nullable(OrderClass.class)`. Practical implication: if your code passes null to a mock method, `any()` won't match in Mockito 2+.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- any(): non-null, any type (Mockito 2+)
- any(ClassName.class): non-null, specific type
- isNull(): matches null
- nullable(ClassName.class): matches null OR ClassName instance
- Mockito 1: any() matched null — behavior changed in v2
- Type-safe matching: any(Order.class) provides better IDE support
- anyString() equivalent to any(String.class) but more explicit
- Use nullable() in production code that accepts null arguments

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: In Mockito 2 and later, any() matches any non-null argument. any(ClassName.class) is the type-safe version — it matches any non-null instance of that class and provides better IDE support and compile-time checking. If a method can be called with null and I want to match that, I use isNull(). If I want to match either null or a non-null object of a type, I use nullable(ClassName.class). This is a behavior change from Mockito 1 where any() matched null too — an important distinction when working with legacy test code.

questions.question: What is ArgumentCaptor and how do you use it?
questions.title: ArgumentCaptor in Mockito
questions.direct_answer: ArgumentCaptor captures the argument passed to a mock method so you can perform assertions on it after the test runs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know how to assert the content of complex objects passed to a dependency
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to assert argument details inside a thenAnswer() instead of using a Captor after verify()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention captor.getAllValues() for cases where the method was called multiple times, and that @Captor annotation is cleaner than ArgumentCaptor.forClass()

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
ArgumentCaptor solves the problem of asserting what argument was actually passed to a mock method. Imagine your service creates an Order object and passes it to orderRepository.save(). You want to verify not just that save was called, but that the Order had the correct status and total. An ArgumentCaptor lets you capture that argument and then run any assertion you like on it.

The pattern has three steps. First, create the captor: either annotate a field with @Captor and annotate the test class with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), or call ArgumentCaptor.forClass(Order.class) manually. Second, use the captor in your verify call: verify(orderRepository).save(captor.capture()). Third, retrieve the captured value and assert: Order captured = captor.getValue(); assertEquals(OrderStatus.CONFIRMED, captured.getStatus()).

If the method was called multiple times you can use captor.getAllValues() which returns a List of all the captured arguments in order.

A word of caution: ArgumentCaptor is most valuable when you need to assert on a complex object. For simple values it is often cleaner to use a specific matcher like verify(mock).save(argThat(order -> order.getStatus() == CONFIRMED)) directly in the verify call.

sections.title: Key Points
content: ArgumentCaptor captures the argument passed to a mock method for post-verification assertions
Three steps: create captor, use captor.capture() in verify(), assert on captor.getValue()
Use captor.getAllValues() when the method was called multiple times
@Captor annotation is cleaner than ArgumentCaptor.forClass() — requires MockitoExtension

followup_questions: When would you use argThat() instead of ArgumentCaptor?
Can you use ArgumentCaptor with @Mock annotations without MockitoExtension?

questions.question: What are the rules for mixing ArgumentMatchers with real values?
questions.title: Mixing ArgumentMatchers with Real Values
questions.direct_answer: You cannot mix ArgumentMatchers and real values in the same method call — either all arguments use matchers or all use real values; wrap real values with eq() when mixing is needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you have hit this common Mockito pitfall and understand the rule behind it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing when(mock.method(anyString(), 42)).thenReturn(x) and getting an InvalidUseOfMatchersException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why Mockito has this constraint: matchers work via thread-local state and mixing raw values bypasses that mechanism

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Mockito has a strict rule: in a single method call used for stubbing or verification, you must use either all ArgumentMatchers or all real values. You cannot mix them. Writing when(mock.method(anyString(), 42)).thenReturn(value) will throw an InvalidUseOfMatchersException at runtime.

The reason is internal: ArgumentMatchers like anyString() and eq() work by pushing a matcher onto a thread-local stack inside Mockito. When you pass a raw value like 42, Mockito has no way to know at the point of stubbing which argument should be matched by a raw value versus a stored matcher, so the counts do not align and it throws an error.

The solution when you need both is to wrap the real value with eq(). So the correct form becomes: when(mock.method(anyString(), eq(42))).thenReturn(value). The eq() matcher matches by equality just like a raw value would, but it participates in the matcher stack properly.

This same rule applies to verify() calls too. If you want to verify a method was called with a specific string and any integer, you write: verify(mock).method(eq("exact-string"), anyInt()).

sections.title: Key Points
content: Cannot mix matchers and raw values in the same stubbing or verify call
Wrap raw values with eq() to use them alongside other matchers: eq("value"), eq(42)
This rule applies to both when() and verify() calls

questions.question: How do you use Mockito's eq() matcher and why is it sometimes necessary when mixing matchers?
questions.title: eq() Matcher and Mixing Rules
questions.direct_answer: eq(value) wraps a literal value as a matcher; you must use it when mixing argument matchers with real values in the same method call, because Mockito requires all arguments to be matchers or none.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Mockito's strict all-or-nothing matcher rule
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing a real value with any() in the same call — Mockito throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate the correct pattern: when(mock.method(eq("id"), any(String.class))).thenReturn(...)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Mockito has a rule that is a frequent source of confusion: in any single method invocation — whether for stubbing or verification — all arguments must either be real values, or all must be argument matchers. You cannot mix them. If you try to write when(mock.find("userId", any(String.class))).thenReturn(...), Mockito will throw an InvalidUseOfMatchersException at runtime.

The fix is eq(). It is an argument matcher that matches using the equals() method — semantically identical to passing the literal value, but it satisfies Mockito's rule that all arguments are matchers. So the correct form is when(mock.find(eq("userId"), any(String.class))).thenReturn(...).

This catches many developers off guard because the error message appears at the next unrelated test rather than at the line that caused it, since Mockito's matcher stack is a thread-local that is drained lazily.

A practical tip: most of the time if you are only using argument matchers for some parameters, you simply need to wrap the literal ones in eq(). Common cases are repository methods that take a fixed ID plus a variable second argument, or service methods that always receive the same enum value but a variable payload.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Mockito rule: all arguments in one call must be matchers or none — no mixing.
eq(value) wraps a literal as a matcher using equals() semantics.
Use eq() when you need at least one real value alongside any(), anyString(), etc.
InvalidUseOfMatchersException often surfaces on the next test line, not the culprit line.

questions.question: How do you write a custom argument matcher using ArgumentMatcher<T> for complex matching logic?
questions.title: Custom ArgumentMatcher
questions.direct_answer: Implement ArgumentMatcher<T> with a matches(T argument) method, then pass it to argThat() in stubbing or verification to apply your custom predicate.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to extend Mockito for domain-specific matching
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing a lambda in argThat() that throws NullPointerException when the argument is null
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both the class-based and lambda forms of argThat(), and mention that null-safety is the caller's responsibility

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When none of Mockito's built-in matchers covers your matching logic, you can create a custom matcher. The interface is ArgumentMatcher<T> and it has one method: boolean matches(T argument). You pass an instance of your matcher to argThat().

You can write it as a named class for complex, reusable logic, or as a lambda for quick inline use. For example, to verify that a saved Order has a non-null ID and a PENDING status: verify(repository).save(argThat(order -> order.getId() != null && order.getStatus() == Status.PENDING)).

One important gotcha: your matches() implementation must handle null gracefully. Mockito may call it with null arguments, especially when checking whether an invocation matches a stubbing. If your lambda does order.getId() without a null check, it throws a NullPointerException and causes confusing test failures. Always guard with a null check: argThat(order -> order != null && order.getId() != null && ...).

For reusable matchers, extract into a named class with a descriptive toString() method. Mockito uses toString() in its error messages when a verification fails, so a good description like 'Order with PENDING status and non-null ID' makes failure messages dramatically easier to understand than the default lambda toString.

ArgumentCaptor is often cleaner for simple field assertions, but argThat() with a custom matcher is more powerful when you need to assert on multiple fields in a single expression without capturing.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Implement ArgumentMatcher<T>.matches() and pass via argThat().
Always null-check inside matches() to avoid NullPointerException.
Override toString() on named matchers for readable failure messages.
